segments.title: Chương 242: Tháp Bảy Tầng
segments.content:
After Andy Lau joined Hai Nei, Sina Blog reacted swiftly.

Just a few days later, before Andy Lau had even pulled his old friends into Hai Nei, Sina Blog brought over a whole package of Emperor Entertainment Group stars.

There was Nicholas Tse, Brother Edison Chen, the Crown Prince of the House of Chan, Eason Chan, Joey Yung, Twins… and so on.

One could only say that Sina really had the clout!

Sohu Blog, reacting a bit late, also went to invite Hong Kong stars to join, but they only managed to pick up a few who were somewhat past their prime.

Blogcn (Blog China) was about to explode. A year ago, its market share exceeded 85%, but now it had plummeted to less than 30%.

Meanwhile, Sina Blog's market share had soared to over 40% in just a few months.

Sohu Blog's market share was just over 20%.

Of course, this didn't include SNS websites with blog functions, such as Xiaonei, Hai Nei, Cyworld, Zhanzuo, QQ Zone, and so on.

NetEase and Baidu were also about to enter the field and were currently developing their own websites—NetEase Blog and Baidu Space.

Basically, whenever something got popular, the major internet companies would flood in.

Chen Guiliang was actually quite similar. When the major internet companies were doing color ringtones, didn't he also excitedly run over to join the fun?

"Xiao Chen, those old friends of mine aren't used to using computers, nor are they familiar with the internet over on the mainland. Only Ada Choi agreed to try Hai Nei," Andy Lau said, calling Chen Guiliang.

The "Empress"?

Chen Guiliang smiled and said, "Whether they're willing to come or not, they're still friends. Thank you for your trouble, Heavenly King Lau."

"Just call me Wah Zai or Andy," Andy Lau said.

Chen Guiliang said, "Then I'll call you Brother Wah."

Although *Crazy Stone* was just one of the projects in Andy Lau's "Focus First Cuts" program, he was paying close attention to it and had even made public appearances to help with its promotion.

However, the publicity and distribution funds were limited, so they didn't even do a proper promotional roadshow.

Let alone any kind of premiere ceremony.

Around the second week of *Crazy Stone*'s release, word-of-mouth began to build within a small circle.

It was particularly buzzing online, especially on Douban. Then there were Xiaonei and Hai Nei.

Chen Guiliang's articles had also helped attract a lot of attention to the movie.

Some cinema chains had already started to increase the number of screenings for *Crazy Stone* and moved them to evening showtimes.

After Ning Hao communicated with Andy Lau, Andy Lau became even more convinced of the internet's usefulness.

Andy Lau said, "Besides Ada Choi, a few of the main actors in the movie I'm currently filming are also planning to join Hai Nei."

"What movie is it?" Chen Guiliang asked.

"*Protégé*. I just joined the cast yesterday," Andy Lau said. "It has Daniel Wu, Zhang Jingchu, Louis Koo, and Anita Yuen."

Louis Koo was a blogging fanatic!

If Chen Guiliang hadn't appeared, Louis Koo would have started blogging on Sina in 2008.

Over twelve years, he wrote 4,434 blog posts. On average, that was one post a day!

When everyone else moved on to Weibo, he continued to post blog articles on Sina.

Zhang Jingchu had already registered on Sina Blog by this time.

This actress was very ambitious, modeling herself after Xu Jinglei. When Xu Jinglei's blog took off, she took the initiative to go to Sina and wrote even more literary-style articles.

But her Sina blog had always been lukewarm.

Now, having joined the cast of *Protégé*, she heard from Andy Lau that Hai Nei was a lot of fun. After carefully learning about Hai Nei, Zhang Jingchu immediately agreed to move from Sina Blog to Hai Nei.

She wanted to become "the Xu Jinglei of Hai Nei"!

Anita Yuen was also an avid blogger. She averaged three posts a month, only stopping after she switched over to Weibo.

As for Daniel Wu, he posted on his blog even more frequently than Anita Yuen, writing about his life, work, friendships, hobbies… he wrote about everything on his blog.

The people Andy Lau pulled into Hai Nei this time were all people who genuinely enjoyed blogging, not just those who did it perfunctorily for work promotions.

When director Derek Yee heard the news, he simply followed suit and registered an account, writing in his very first post: "Hello everyone, I'm Derek Yee. The cast and crew of *Protégé* have all joined Hai Nei. We hope our fellow netizens will follow this movie, which is expected to be released next year."

With several celebrities arriving at once, their Hai Nei homepages became especially lively.

Chen Guiliang also went to leave comments.

He even specifically wrote on Daniel Wu's message board: "Hello, I'm Daniel Wu from Peking University. How come you have this name too?"

A bunch of netizens teased and mocked: "Chen Shiyi is so shameless. I'm Takeshi Kaneshiro from Northeast China!"

"Daniel Wu from West Yunnan reporting for duty!"

"So many people with the same name. I also happen to be called Daniel Wu from Pudong."

Damn it, everyone was playing along with the meme.

As more and more celebrities joined Hai Nei, their biggest competitor, Cyworld, also reacted.

Since *My Bratty Princess* was very popular this year, Cyworld invited Korean star Jang Na-ra to join.

This was in line with Cyworld's usual style of attracting users through the "Korean Wave." The effect was excellent, with registered users already exceeding 1.5 million.

But the concentration of a large number of Korean Wave fans also annoyed many netizens, who claimed they would never use Cyworld even if it killed them.

"Huh, Chen Xiaoxu's account hasn't been updated in over half a month?" Chen Guiliang was hopping between celebrity homepages when he suddenly noticed Chen Xiaoxu's situation.

Chen Guiliang took out his phone and called Professor Lou, his *History of Chinese Philosophy* teacher.

This Professor Lou was the director of the Oriental Philosophy Department at Peking University's Philosophy Department and the honorary dean of the Institute for the Study of Religion at Peking University.

"Professor Lou, hello, this is Chen Guiliang," Chen Guiliang said.

Professor Lou chuckled, "You did alright on the exam this time. Even without special treatment, you wouldn't have failed *History of Chinese Philosophy*."

What the!

Is this really the impression I've made on all the professors?

The first thing they say on the phone is about whether I'll fail.

"That's thanks to Professor Lou's great skill. One of your lectures is worth ten others, which is why I did so well on the final."

After a quick bit of flattery, Chen Guiliang got to the point: "I have a friend who is a Buddhist. She has breast cancer but is unwilling to cooperate with treatment. One moment she says Buddhism is about letting nature take its course, that life and death are fated. The next moment she says that a mastectomy would look terrible, that she would no longer be beautiful. How can I use Buddhist teachings to persuade her?"

Professor Lou immediately became serious. "Buddhism certainly doesn't support refusing treatment for an illness. Wait a moment, I'll look up Buddhist scriptures related to healing. I guarantee I'll find well-founded arguments to help you persuade your friend to get treatment."

"Thank you so much, Professor Lou," Chen Guiliang said gratefully.

Two days later, Chen Guiliang received an email from Professor Lou.

The information was so detailed it could have been used to write a thesis!

Chen Guiliang had Chen Xiaoxu's phone number. After reading through the Buddhist materials, he sent her a text message: "Sister Xiaoxu, how come your Hai Nei hasn't been updated in over half a month?"

"I've been busy lately." Chen Xiaoxu didn't mention that she had cancer.

Chen Guiliang couldn't be bothered to beat around the bush and texted directly: "In the Ekottara Āgama, the Buddha taught: 'Sickness is remedied by medicine.' The Buddha said that when you are sick, you should receive treatment."

"Who told you I was sick????" Chen Xiaoxu sent back a string of question marks.
